subject: Biology
title: Respiration in Plants
summary: Cellular respiration breaks down food (mainly glucose) to release energy, trapped as ATP. Plants have no special respiratory organs; each part exchanges gases by diffusion through stomata and lenticels.
Glycolysis (EMP pathway) in the cytoplasm splits glucose into two pyruvate. Without O₂, pyruvate is fermented to ethanol (yeast) or lactic acid (muscle, bacteria).
With O₂, pyruvate enters mitochondria: link reaction → Krebs cycle (matrix) → electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane). O₂ is the final electron acceptor.
Respiration is amphibolic — it both breaks down and builds molecules. The respiratory quotient (RQ) depends on the substrate.

formulas.name: Glycolysis
formulas.formula: glucose → 2 pyruvate;  net gain 2 ATP + 2 NADH;  uses 2 ATP (hexokinase, phosphofructokinase), makes 4 ATP
formulas.note: Glycolysis is the only process common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

formulas.name: Fermentation
formulas.formula: yeast: pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂ → ethanol (pyruvic acid decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase);  muscle/bacteria: pyruvate → lactic acid (lactate dehydrogenase)
formulas.note: Yeasts poison themselves when ethanol reaches about 13%.

formulas.name: Link reaction
formulas.formula: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH (pyruvate dehydrogenase, in mitochondrial matrix)

formulas.name: Krebs (TCA) cycle per acetyl CoA
formulas.formula: acetyl CoA (2C) + OAA (4C) → citric acid (6C) … → OAA;  gives 2 CO₂ + 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 ATP (GTP)

formulas.name: ETS sequence
formulas.formula: NADH → complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) → ubiquinone → complex III (cyt bc₁) → cytochrome c → complex IV (cyt a–a₃, Cu centres) → O₂;  FADH₂ enters at complex II

formulas.name: ATP yield per carrier
formulas.formula: 1 NADH → 3 ATP;  1 FADH₂ → 2 ATP (complex V — ATP synthase F₀–F₁)

formulas.name: Net ATP from one glucose
formulas.note: Real yields are lower; 38 is a theoretical value assuming a sequential pathway.

formulas.name: Respiratory quotient
formulas.formula: RQ = volume of CO₂ evolved / volume of O₂ consumed

formulas.name: RQ values
formulas.formula: carbohydrates = 1;  fats ≈ 0.7;  proteins ≈ 0.9;  organic acids (malic) > 1;  anaerobic = ∞ (CO₂ but no O₂)

formulas.name: Amphibolic pathway
formulas.formula: fats → glycerol (→ PGAL) + fatty acids (→ acetyl CoA);  proteins → amino acids → pyruvate/acetyl CoA/Krebs intermediates

examples.title: ATP from one glucose
examples.problem: Count the theoretical ATP from one glucose in aerobic respiration.
examples.solution: Glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (6 ATP); link reaction 2 NADH (6 ATP); Krebs cycle 6 NADH (18 ATP) + 2 FADH₂ (4 ATP) + 2 ATP. Total = 38 ATP.

examples.title: RQ of malic acid
examples.solution: RQ = 4/3 = 1.33 — more than 1, as for organic acids.

examples.title: Muscle cramps
examples.problem: Why do muscles feel tired after heavy exercise?
examples.solution: When O₂ is insufficient, muscle cells reduce pyruvate to lactic acid (anaerobic), which accumulates and causes fatigue.

examples.title: Final electron acceptor
examples.problem: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?
examples.solution: Oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons at the end of the ETS; it combines with protons to form water. Without it, the chain stops and ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation ceases.

examples.title: Respiration is amphibolic
examples.problem: Why is respiration called an amphibolic pathway?
examples.solution: Its intermediates are used both in breakdown (catabolism) and in synthesis (anabolism) — e.g. acetyl CoA is used for fatty acid synthesis and Krebs intermediates for amino acids.

topics.title: Gas exchange in plants
topics.explain: Plants get O₂ through stomata and lenticels; living cells of stems and roots lie close to the surface, and most cells have at least part of their surface in contact with air. Gas exchange needs are low compared with animals.

topics.title: Steps of glycolysis
topics.explain: Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (ATP used) → fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (ATP used) → DHAP + 3-PGAL → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (NADH formed) → 3-PGA (ATP) → 2-PGA → PEP → pyruvate (ATP).

topics.title: Krebs cycle details
topics.explain: Discovered by Hans Krebs. Citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (CO₂, NADH) → succinyl CoA (CO₂, NADH) → succinate (GTP/ATP — substrate-level phosphorylation) → fumarate (FADH₂) → malate → OAA (NADH).

topics.title: Oxidative phosphorylation
topics.explain: Energy from electron transport pumps protons into the intermembrane space; the gradient drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through F₀ (channel) to F₁ (headpiece, catalytic site) of ATP synthase.

topics.title: Assumptions of the 38 ATP count
topics.explain: A sequential, orderly pathway; NADH from glycolysis enters mitochondria and is fully oxidised; no intermediates are used for other compounds; only glucose is respired. In reality none of these fully hold.

topics.title: Fermentation vs aerobic respiration
topics.explain: Fermentation partially breaks down glucose, gives net 2 ATP and NADH is re-oxidised to NAD⁺ slowly; aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose to CO₂ and water, yielding far more ATP.

ratta: Krebs per acetyl CoA: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP.
Complex IV: cyt a–a₃ + Cu;  complex V: ATP synthase.
RQ: carb 1, fat 0.7, protein 0.9, malic acid 1.33.
Yeast → ethanol + CO₂;  muscle → lactic acid.
